article.headline: AI Agents Vindicate the Product Owner's Playbook
article.lede: A developer's rueful one-liner — "so maybe the product owners were on to something" — is also a sharp observation about the emerging grammar of AI-assisted software development. The attached image is a prompt handed to an AI coding agent, instructing it to decompose a project spec into sprints and tickets: each task **atomic and committable**, each sprint ending in deployable software. It reads, essentially, like a scrum master's brief.
article.body:
The prompt's logic is tight. Every ticket must be small enough to constitute a single commit and must carry explicit tests or an equivalent validation criterion. Sprints must yield software that "can be run, tested, and built upon" — the textbook definition of a *shippable increment* in agile methodology. A subagent is then invoked to review the plan before anything is written to disk. The whole sequence mimics the planning ceremonies that many engineers have long dismissed as bureaucratic theatre.

What changed is the executor. A human developer handed a vague multi-week spec can ask clarifying questions, hold context across days, and course-correct mid-stream. An AI coding agent cannot. Without tight scope it will drift, overreach, or produce a thousand-line diff that is nearly impossible to review. Dillon Mulroy, a Principal Engineer at Cloudflare who has spoken publicly about **Agent Experience** — the discipline of designing workflows that AI agents can navigate reliably — has noted that agents "tempt you to ship huge diffs overnight." Structured decomposition is the antidote.

The subagent review step is itself notable. Rather than trusting a single model pass, the workflow routes the initial plan to a second agent for critique before committing anything to a file. It mirrors the peer-review step in human engineering but executes in seconds. It also hedges against a known failure mode: AI agents tend to ratify the framing of the task they are given, so an independent reviewer — even a stateless one — can surface blind spots the first pass missed.

The broader implication is that good *prompt engineering* for agentic coding converges on the same principles agile practitioners have advocated for decades: small scope, clear acceptance criteria, incremental delivery. The developer instinct to resist process in favor of flow works when the craftsperson is human and can hold a mental model across a week. When the craftsperson is an agent with no persistent memory and a tendency toward confident overreach, structure stops being overhead and becomes load-bearing infrastructure.

concepts.definition: An atomic ticket is a unit of work small enough to be completed in a single, coherent commit. The goal is that it can be reviewed, tested, and reverted in isolation. Atomicity reduces integration risk and makes progress measurable — qualities that matter even more when the worker is an AI agent that cannot hold context across sessions.

A shippable increment is a version of software that is fully functional and demonstrable at the end of a sprint, even if the overall product is unfinished. It must be buildable and runnable by stakeholders — not a partial stub. The concept comes from the Scrum agile framework and is the basis for iterative delivery.

Agent Experience is the emerging discipline of designing systems, APIs, and workflows so that AI coding agents can use them reliably. It draws on the same principles as developer experience (DX) but accounts for failure modes specific to language-model agents: context loss, overconfidence, and scope creep. Dillon Mulroy has discussed it publicly in the context of Cloudflare's internal platform work.

A subagent is an AI model instance spawned by a parent agent to perform a specific subtask — here, reviewing a sprint plan for gaps. The pattern is common in multi-agent architectures and is used to parallelize work or introduce a second opinion without adding human review latency.
